‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled By Amazon After One Season

Matt SingerPublished: September 4, 2026
  • Share on Facebook
  • Share on Twitter

Instaread

Spider-Man: Brand New Day may be one of the biggest movies ever, but not every Spidey title is a hit.

Amazon has canceled their Spider-Noir live-action TV show starring Nicolas Cage after only one season, according to Variety,

The show was developed by Oren Uziel and starred Cage as Ben Reilly, a private eye who is secretly a superhero in 1930s New York City. Its cast also included Lamorne Morris, Li Jun Li, and Brendan Gleeson.

The show was also notable for being presented simultaneously in color or black and white episodes, with the viewer allowed to pick which version they wanted to watch.

I guess that gimmick wasn’t enough to entice viewers, nor was the appeal of Cage, the voice of the animated Spider-Man Nori in the Into and Across the Spider-Verse movies, playing the live-action version of the same characters. (Spider-Noir was executive produced by Spider-Verse’s Amy Pascal, Phil Lord, and Chris Miller.)

READ MORE: Every Spider-Man Movie and Spinoff Ranked From Worst to Best

Spider-Noir was created as part of a deal between Sony and Amazon to develop Spider-Man show to compliment Sony’s Spidey movies. But it now ends after producing only eight episodes. We’ll have to see whether any other Spider-Man (or Spider-Man adjacent) TV shows make their way to streaming on Prime Video.

Sony’s riding high on the record-breaking success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which is already the highest-grossing Spider-Man film in the character’s history. But Sony hasn’t released a Spidey spinoff movie in almost two years. In 2024, they released three different films in their Spider-Man universe: Madame Web, Venom: The Last Dance, and Kraven the Hunter. 

Although Last Dance performed reasonably well in theaters, it was also the lowest-grossing film in the Venom series, and Madame Web and Kraven the Hunter were both flops and among the worst-reviewed superhero movies in history. So the company is still searching for a way to translate the success of the main Spider-Man (and Spider-Verse) movies to a broader Spider-Man universe.

The Greatest Spider-Man Comic Covers Ever

We went through 1000 issues of Amazing Spider-Man and countless other Spidey series to pick the 100 best covers ever.

Marvel

100. The Amazing Spider-Man Super Special #1 (1995)

Cover Artist: Steve Lightle

C’mon it’s not just a planet of symbiotes — it’s a planet that looks like Venom’s snarling face. How do you not love that?

Marvel

99. Spider-Man: Revenge of the Green Goblin #3 (2000)

Cover Artist: Ron Frenz

Yeah, Venom is a symbiote, but Spider-Man’s most symbiotic relationship with a villain must surely be with Norman Osborn, AKA the Green Goblin, who has at times been his bitterest adversary, and at others one of his closest allies. (He even became Spider-Man for a period recently.) This cover captures the intensity of that relationship in one striking image.

Marvel

98. The Sentry/Spider-Man #1 (2001)

Cover Artist: Rick Leonardi

Spider-Man and photographs go together like Power Man and Iron Fist, and this bold collage piece nicely incorporates that aspect of the character into its visual storytelling.

Marvel

97. Marvel Team-Up #74 (1978)

Cover Artist: Dave Cockrum

Each issue of Marvel Team-Up paired Spider-Man with a different guest star. Typically the guest was another Marvel hero — but for one very surreal month in 1978, he partnered with the original cast of Saturday Night Live. The likenesses to Belushi, Aykroyd, and the rest aren’t perfect, but the composition with Belushi’s Samurai squaring off with an barely seen Silver Samurai is delightful, as is the touch of Japanese dialogue in Belushi’s word balloon.

Marvel

96. Spider-Man Unlimited #7 (1994)

Cover Artist: Ron Lim

Spider-Man comics of the mid-1990s were dominated by the notorious “Clone Saga,” a lot of which was surreal and bizarre — with garish art to match. But this cover for the quarterly Spider-Man Unlimited series, bisecting Spider-Man and his clone, the Scarlet Spider, as two halves of a whole, is a really handsome piece (especially for a comic with two stories, one starring each of the two heroes).

Marvel

95. Giant-Size Spider-Man #4 (1975)

Cover Artist: Gil Kane

Talk about a nightmarish image — Spider-Man snarled in a barbed-wire fence, waiting for a rescue from the Punisher. The text box reads “AT LAST! The wonderous web-slinger and gangland’s executioner join forces to SAVE THE WORLD!” That’d get my 50 cents any day of the week and twice on Wednesdays..

Marvel/DC

94. Spider-Man and Batman #1 (1995)

Cover Artist: Mark Bagley

The illustrations of Spidey and the Dark Knight are good, but it’s the Bat-Signal with spider webs really puts this crossover cover over the top.

Marvel

93. Peter Parker: Spider-Man #21 (2000)

Cover Artist: Mark Buckingham

The Human Torch and Spider-Man have a history in Marvel Comics going back decades, and they’ve shared several memorable covers in that time. That includes this one by Marcos Martin from the brief period when the Torch “died,” along with this simple but eye-catching piece with both characters high in the air — Spidey stuck to a building, Johnny Storm floating beside him — while they stare down the reader.

Marvel

92. Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #112 (1985)

Cover Artist: Kyle Baker

Unless you count the corner box, there}s no Spider-Man on this cover. But there is a Santa Claus smoking a cigarette and brandishing a massive handgun. And sometimes, that’s more than enough.

Marvel

91. The Amazing Spider-Man #9 (2014)

Cover Artist: Olivier Coipel

The original “Spider-Verse” storyline kicks off in this issue of The Amazing Spider-Man, covered by this beautifully laid-out assembly of webbed heroes by Olivier Coipel.

Marvel

90. Spidey Super Stories #16 (1976)

Cover Artist: John Romita

This delightful series for kids inspired by the 1970s PBS show The Electric Company sported several pop culture parody covers — like this one inspired by Jaws. Frankly I’d rather see this story as a movie than the ones in several Jaws sequels.

Marvel

89. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #2 (1965)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

Steve Ditko defined Spider-Man’s unnaturally spindly physicality, and there’s a little of that here in the smaller Spidey surrounding that big headshot at the center of this piece. But the full-body shot of Spider-Man, striking a simple but heroic pose, really stands out. It conveys a stoic power that’s lacking from a lot of even the best Spidey covers.

Marvel

88. The Amazing Spider-Man #619 (2010)

Cover Artist: Marcos Martin

The best modern Spider-Man cover artist might be Marcos Martin, and he will be very well-represented on this list, starting with this intensely moody piece from the “Brand New Day” era of Spidey history. The color dripping from the logo onto Spider-Man and the bodies at his feet is just an incredible concept, and one perfectly executed by Martin and colorist Javier Rodríg﻿uez.

Marvel

87. Spider-Man: With Great Power... #1 (2008)

Cover Artist: Tony Harris

I’m a sucker for any image of Peter Parker and Spider-Man split down the middle, sharing a single body; it’s the visual representation of the central conflict in just about every Spider-Man comic ever published. This one by Tony Harris is very well laid out, and the crossed arms (one with a spider in the palm, the other striking a classic “THWIP!” pose) is not only visually arresting, it further muddies the line between Peter and Spider-Man in a way that almost suggests an Ouroboros.

Marvel

86. The Amazing Spider-Man #100 (1971)

Cover Artist: John Romita

This iconic anniversary cover by the great John Romita has been imitated and reprinted countless times — I own a T-shirt of this cover I bought at Target — which is a tribute to its enormous visual impact.

Marvel

85. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #42 (2018)

Cover Artist: Alex Ross

Although he’s never drawn a monthly Spider-Man series, Alex Ross has contributed a ton of signature Spider-Man images in recent years, mostly through his work on Amazing Spider-Man covers. A lot of them look like they could be movie posters, including this one with Spider-Man swinging past the Daily Bugle, where Ross has shaded in images of the staff, including Betty Brant and Robbie Robertson.

Marvel

84. Peter Parker: The Spectacular Spider-Man #3 (2017)

Cover Artist: Mark Bagley

Few artists in the last 30 years have left a bigger legacy on Spider-Man’s visual representation than Mark Bagley, who had a terrific run on The Amazing Spider-Man in the mid-1990s and then an even more impactful time on Ultimate Spider-Man in the 2000s. But one of his best covers came after his monthly work on Spidey came to an end, with this variant cover from the 2010s short-lived Spectacular Spider-Man revival. It boasts a very unique perspective, and has the added whimsical touch of Spidey munching a slice of pizza as he races up the side of a skyscraper.

Marvel

83. The Amazing Spider-Man #315 (1989)

Cover Artist: Todd McFarlane

Hydro-Man — a villain who can transform his body into water — does not sound like a particularly intimidating foe for a guy like Spider-Man, but this piece by Todd McFarlane presents him as a real threat, with Spidey about to drown inside a big pool of Hydro-Man guts (ew). Bonus points here for the playful use of Venom in the text box, who responds to Hydro-Man declaring that he “wins at last!!” with a dismissive “Yeah, right!”

Marvel

82. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #19 (1985)

Cover Artist: Mary Wilshire

“This is a job for ...” Mary Jane?!? As sales pitches for Spider-Man annuals go, that — along with this nicely penciled piece by Mary Wilshire spoofing the iconic image of Clark Kent ripping open his suit to reveal his Superman costume — is about as good as it gets.

Marvel

81. The Amazing Spider-Man #78 (2021)

Cover Artist: Arthur Adams

Arthut Adams had a string of superb covers during the recent “Beyond” era of The Amazing Spider-Man. The best of the best is this one, which integrates the book’s logo into the layout in the form of a neon street sign beneath a crouched Spider-Man. Something activates his Spider-Sense, but what? Readers can see it’s the living vampire Morbius, lurking just behind our hero, waiting to strike. Watch out Spidey!

Marvel

80. The Amazing Spider-Man #34 (1965)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

Obviously this is not the most detailed piece in Steve Ditko’s portfolio — the buildings bear just a handful of lines and the sky is a blank white. But that serves to focus all the attention on the two figures on this cover, both of whom are glorious. You have Spider-Man posed in terror and anticipation as Kraven the Hunter descends from above. I love the detail of his lion’s mane vest flapping behind him, conveying the intense speed of his fall.

Marvel

79. The Amazing Spider-Man #531 (2006)

Cover Artist: Ron Garney

Peter Parker’s life got pretty surreal in the run-up to the Civil War crossover series. He joined the Avengers, revealed his secret identity to the world, was gifted an armored costume by Iron Man inventor Tony Stark, and moved into Avengers Tower with Mary Jane and Aunt May. This deadpan cover, with Spidey catching some TV time with Stark and Captain America, nicely summarizes just how strange this period was.

Marvel

78. Marvel Team-Up #132 (1983)

Cover Artist: Paul Smith

Illustrator Paul Smith is best known at Marvel for his time on Uncanny X-Men. He never did much Spider-Man work — which is a darn shame, given the beauty of this rare piece from the cover of Marvel Team-Up #132. I love the webby line work on Spider-Man’s costume and eyes here. This guy should have drawn more Spider-Man!

Marvel

77. The Amazing Spider-Man #229 (1982)

Cover Artist: John Romita Jr.

This issue written by Roger Stern with Spider-Man versus the X-Men villain the Juggernaut is seen as something of a character-defining storyline by Spidey fans; showing that even when faced with a far more powerful and possibly unstoppable foe, Spidey refuses to quit or give up. This simple but effective cover by the great John Romita Jr. establishes Juggernaut’s power and threat through the characters’ positioning and body language.

Marvel

76. The Amazing Spider-Man #1 (2015)

Cover Artist: Alex Ross

Alex Ross designed this underrated costume from the “Parker Industries” era of The Amazing Spider-Man, when Peter launched his own company based on his incredible technological inventions. This cover showcases that cool new costume (complete with glowy spider emblem), a new Spider-Mobile, and even a shot of Peter going full James Bond in a tuxedo with women on each arm. It foreshadows just how different this run of Spider-Man will be from the classical interpretation, where he’s much more of a lovable loser with a habit of screwing up his life in 500 different ways simultaneously.

Marvel

75. Amazing Spider-Man: Family Business (2014)

Cover Artist: Gabrielle Dell’Otto and Werther Dell'Edera

This 2014 graphic novel sports a really dynamic fully painted cover, with blocks of red and white standing in contrast with the flowery print on the Kingpin’s shirt.

Marvel

74. The Amazing Spider-Man #546 (2008)

Cover Artist: Steve McNiven

The back-to-basics era of “Brand New Day” kicked off in this issue, sporting about as classical image of Spider-Man as you’ll find on a Spider-Man comic published in the 21st century. There’s a lot of speed and movement captured in Steve McNiven’s line work, from Peter pulling down his mask to his camera dangling precariously off his shoulder.

Marvel

73. Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man #20 (2007)

Cover Artist: Tomm Coker

Spider-Man’s black costume always looks good on a stark black and white cover. This one pairs it with a dramatic web and an upside-down Spider-Man for a particularly spidery image that works well with the moodier stories of the “Back in Black” era.

Marvel

72. Spider-Man and the X-Men #6 (2015)

Cover Artist: Stacey Lee

This underrated series from 2015 saw Spider-Man become a substitute teacher at the X-Men’s School for Gifted Youngsters. What better image for the final issue than a class photo? It’s an obvious idea, but it’s also a superb execution by Stacey Lee, with terrific pencils in the faces and poses of the young X-Men.

Marvel

71. The Amazing Spider-Man #52 (1967)

Cover Artist: John Romita

John Romita’s artwork stands the test of time because it was packed with so much energy and intensity. This cover is like an amazing cliffhanger in a single image, with Spidey and his perpetual adversary, J. Jonah Jameson, chained together surrounded by rising waters. You don’t want to find out how Spidey wriggles out of this trap; you need to know.

Marvel

70. Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #64 (1982)

Cover Artist: Ed Hannigan

This is just me speaking here: I love covers that integrate text into the action — like this one does in introducing Cloak and Dagger to the Marvel Universe. (The drippy treatment of the comic’s title adds a moody touch as well.)

Marvel

69. Superior Spider-Man Team-Up #5 (2013)

Cover Artist: Paolo & Joe Rivera

During the Superior Spider-Man era, Doctor Octopus managed to implant his own consciousness into Peter Parker’s body, and take over his life for a time. Hence this cover, with the sublime touch of Doc Ock’s tentacles in a claw game pulling at various villains — an allegory for this amoral Spider-Man assembling a team of mind-controlled baddies he leads as “The Superior Six.”

Marvel

68. The Amazing Spider-Man #31 (2023)

Cover Artist: Jim Cheung

The only sight more common on a Spider-Man cover than Spider-Man himself is The Amazing Spider-Man logo. But over 60+ years it’s rarely been seen like this, at such an extreme angle, filling up so much of the artwork, and with Spider-Man singing directly in front of it. It takes a lot to create a Spider-Man cover that feels truly new in the 2020s, but Jim Cheung pulled it off with this variant.

Marvel

67. Web of Spider-Man #12 (1985)

Cover Artist: Mark Beachum

A perfect cover concept: Mary Jane looking for Peter Parker, without realizing a gunman is hiding just behind the door — while Spider-Man lurks outside the apartment window. The ironic word balloons (She’s going to make Peter have fun “even if it KILLS me!”) are the icing on the cake.

Marvel

66. Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #97 (1984)

Cover Artist: Al Milgrom

This was a comic I owned as a child, mostly because this image grabbed me when I saw it on a supermarket magazine shelf and I begged my mother to buy it for me. The cover was a bit of a bait and switch; the issue’s not about some all-powerful Hermit. It’s mostly about Spider-Man’s symbiotic black costume; the “Hermit” was just an ad man who wanted to be left alone and gets a little bit of valuable advice from Spidey. Still: What a gorgeous, atmospheric cover.

Marvel

65. The Amazing Spider-Man #801 (2018)

Cover Artist: Marcos Martin

Dan Slott bid farewell to his epic run on The Amazing Spider-Man with this emotional exclamation point about Spider-Man’s impact on people’s lives, both on and off the comics page. Once again, Marcos Martin found precisely the right image to sum up that sentiment.

Marvel

64. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #1 (1964)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

The ultimate team of Spider-Man villains, the Sinister Six, debuted in the first-ever Spider-Man annual. Steve Ditko got to put his stamp on this group with appealing drawings of all six members, along with a great Spider-Man in the foreground. I especially like the gloppy, gloopy Sandman who really looks like a sentient pile of muck here.

Marvel

63. The Amazing Spider-Man #55 (2020)

Cover Artist: Patrick Gleason

We’ve seen Spider-Man swinging from and surrounded by plenty of webs already on this list, but this innovative cover by Patrick Gleason combines the two into a single visual idea: A Spider-Man composed entirely out of webs. An image where you can peer directly through Spider-Man and see what lies beneath the surface also fits for a Spidey storyline like “Last Remains,” about a mysterious villain with ties to Peter Parker’s past.

Marvel

62. The Amazing Spider-Man: Renew Your Vows #13 (2017)

Cover Artist: Michael Walsh

Renew Your Vows was a fun alternate reality series about a world where Spider-Man, Mary Jane, and their daughter Annie operate as a whole family of superheroes. This appealing variant cover by Michael Walsh captures the romanticism baked into the concept of a hero getting to save the world with his wife and daughter by his side.

Marvel

61. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #5 (1968)

Cover Artist: John Romita

The mystery of Peter Parker’s parents loomed over the early years of The Amazing Spider-Man comics. Their story was finally told in this annual, with an appropriately ominous cover from John Romita filled with the faces of the book’s entire cast swirling through a vertiginous abyss. (Note also the white silhouettes of Richard and Mary Parker standing in the distance.)

Marvel

60. Spider-Men #2 (2012)

Cover Artist: Sara Pichelli

The threat of Spider-Man’s losing his mask equals instant cover drama. Sara Pichelli doubles the danger with this cover for the crossover series Spider-Men, which featured the first meeting between Peter Parker and Miles Morales.

Marvel

59. The Spectacular Spider-Man #1 (1968)

Cover Artist: Harry Rosenbaum

This eye-catching piece has been imitated and homaged by other artists many times through the years. (Alex Ross painted his own beautiful interpretation of it for his variant cover to Peter Parker: The Spectacular Spider-Man #300.) The combination of a very spidery pose and a spotlight shining down on our web-slinger, makes for a very evocative piece.

Marvel

58. The Amazing Spider-Man #29 (1965)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

Between Spider-Man and Scorpion and the swooshing and swirling water, there is just so much kinetic energy flying off this Steve Ditko cover from 1965. But whatever you do ... wherever you go ... just remember: never step on a scorpion!

Marvel

57. The Amazing Spider-Man #300 (1988)

Cover Artist: Todd McFarlane

Another Spider-Man image that has been imitated and duplicated and merchandised an endless number of times — including by the artist himself. Todd McFarlane copied his own physics-defying image of a mid-swing Spidey with the very next Amazing Spider-Man cover he drew, which featured Spider-Man in the exact same pose in his traditional red-and-blue costume. McFarlane’s toy company has also released a Spider-Man statue of this image as well.

Marvel

56. The Amazing Spider-Man #278 (1986)

Cover Artist: Mike Harris

The mystery of the Hobgoblin’s secret identity cast a long shadow over Spider-Man comics in the mid-1980s, including this one involving one of the many fake-outs where it seemed liked Hobgoblin’s identity was revealed (as Peter Parker’s old high-school bully Flash Thompson, in this case), only for it to turn out to be another red herring engineered by the “real” Hobgoblin as part of his evil schemes. Justice wasn’t technically served here, but it does make for an unforgettable cover anyway.

Marvel

55. Spider-Man’s Tangled Web #10 (2002)

Cover Artist: Kaare Andrews

Kaare Andrews’ cover for the Spider-Man anthology comic Tangled Web captures the way so many children were incepted with a love of Spider-Man over the years: By discovering him as a Saturday morning cartoon character. The details here — the open box of cereal, the glow reflecting off the young boy’s shoulder from the television — makes it feel like something plucked from a lived-in memory.

Marvel

54. The Amazing Spider-Man #252 (1984)

Cover Artist: Ron Frenz

To introduce Spider-Man’s new black costume, Ron Frenz recreated Jack Kirby’s signature cover for Amazing Fantasy #15 ((which, uh, spoiler alert, we will get to), this time with Spider-Man in his new black costume. Set against a red and yellow sunset, the debut of the new Spider-Man conveys this aura of power and mystery.

Marvel

53. Spider-Man #57 (1995)

Cover Artist: John Romita Jr.

There have been a fair number of Spider-Man in prison covers through the years. This one by John Romita Jr. earns bonus points because in its original printing it was actually a die-cut cover, with the prison bars printed an added exterior layer that lay on top of the art by Romita of Peter Parker in his cell.

Marvel

52. Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #77 (1983)

Cover Artist: Al Milgrom

The Gladiator is an obscure Marvel villain typically garbed in garish yellows and blues, a big helmet, and enormous forearm blades. Frankly, he looks really silly, but you wouldn’t know it from this Al Milgrom cover, where he demolishes The Spectacular Spider-Man logo as he swings at a leaping Spidey.

Marvel

51. Untold Tales of Spider-Man #7 (1996)

Cover Artist: Pat Olliffe

Untold Tales of Spider-Man is one of the great unsung chapters of Spider-Man history. This 1990s book inserted never-before-told stories into the early years of Amazing Spider-Man continuity; each issue took place at a specific point between certain Lee/Ditko comics. Best of all, it only cost 99 cents a month at a time when a lot of Marvel books were double that price. Artist Pat Olliffe did an outstanding job of evoking Steve Ditko’s style without openly copying it, as seen on this top-notch cover depicting an unseen character peering at a photograph of Spidey through a magnifying glass.

Marvel

50. The Amazing Spider-Man #11 (1999)

Cover Artist: John Byrne

In the wake of the notorious “Clone Saga,” creative control of the Spider-Man books was handed to John Byrne in what was intended as a sort of soft reboot and a back-to-basics approach to the character akin to Byrne’s landmark run on DC’s Superman titles. The results weren’t quite as successful, or as popular with readers, but Byrne did some handsome work during this era, and this unusual piece, with a smooshed Spidey beneath the foot of the bloated X-Men villain the Blob, stands out as a highlight.

Marvel

49. The Amazing Spider-Man #347 (1991)

Cover Artist: Erik Larsen

The Amazing Spider-Man is a long-form Shakespearean tragedy. Don‘t believe me? Check out this hilarious cover by Erik Larsen. (Somehow, this image does actually appear in this issue, too.)

Marvel

48. Spider-Man/Deadpool #48 (2019)

Cover Artist: Will Robson

One of the unwritten rules of comic covers: The more important the character, they bigger they are typically drawn. You don’t want potential customers squinting as they peruse the new release wall at their local shop. But playing with that unwritten rule on occasion can yield clever results, as in this this cover to the Spider-Man/Deadpool series of the 2010s. The issue is a tie-in with the “War of the Realms” crossover, when Earth was invaded by the Thor baddie Malekith. Here the microscopic Spidey and Deadpool show just how enormous and overwhelming Malekith’s otherworldly forces are.

DC/Marvel

47. Superman vs. the Amazing Spider-Man #1 (1976)

Cover Artist: Carmine Infantino and Ross Andru

The stars of two comic universes met for the first time on this instantly iconic jam cover by DC’s Carmine Infantino and Marvel’s Ross Andru. I love the skewed perspective so that Spider-Man looks like he’s standing vertically even though he’s actually leaning off the top of a skyscraper at close to a 90 degree angle, fists coiled and prepared for a fight with the Man of Steel.

Marvel

46. The Amazing Spider-Man #700 (2012)

Cover Artist: Pascal Garcin

To celebrate The Amazing Spider-Man’s milestone 700th issue, Marvel recruited artist Pascal Garcin to craft this spectacular (and sensational) collage pieced together out of hundreds of Spider-Mans and Venoms and assorted other characters in black and white. It also works well with the story beneath the cover, in which Peter Parker’s world is shattered into a million pieces after Doctor Octopus engineers his ultimate scheme for revenge against the Wall-Crawler.

Marvel

45. The Amazing Spider-Man #131 (1974)

Cover Artist: Gil Kane

An undeniably campy cover, but one that’s fully aware of its own absurdity. You know how I know? The priest in the extreme foreground saying “With this ring, I thee — web?” as Spidey’s swings towards his Bible. That pun belongs in the Dad Joke Hall of Fame.

Marvel

44. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #21 (1987)

Cover Artist: John Romita

John Romita actually drew two different covers for the famous Amazing Spider-Man annual featuring the wedding of Peter Parer and Mary Jane Watson: One with Spider-Man and his bride between an assembly of Marvel heroes and villains, and one with Peter and MJ flanked by The Amazing Spider-Man’s supporting cast of characters. Both are nice, but I’ve always preferred this one for the sheer incongruity of the sight of a woman in a dazzling designer gown hanging off the arm of a dude in head-to-toe Spandex. (It also echoes the wedding publicity stunt that Marvel held to promote the issue at Shea Stadium.)

Marvel

43. Peter Parker #4 (2010)

Cover Artist: Brendan McCarthy

The practicalities of the life of a superhero are only occasionally addressed in comics. For a guy like Spider-Man — who is mostly portrayed as a bachelor whose double life already makes him one of the busiest men on the planet — the question of how to clean his costume is one that is often ignored. He can’t go to the laundromat! In most storylines he’s way too poor to own a laundry machine! Hence a cover like this one from Peter Parker #4.

Marvel

42. The Amazing Spider-Man #575 (2008)

Cover Artist: Chris Bachalo

Ow.

Marvel

41. The Amazing Spider-Man #608 (2009)

Cover Artist: Adi Granov

Best known for art that helped inspire and define the look of Iron Man in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Bosnian artist and painter Adi Granov also contributed this stellar Spidey cover featuring the villain known as Raptor, who is out for revenge against Spider-Man’s clone Ben Reilly, hence the subtle differences between the two halves of the photograph Raptor is ripping in this piece. The left side features Spider-Man in his traditional costume; the right side shows Spider-Man in the suit worn by Reilly in his brief tenure as the Web-Slinger.

Marvel

40. Marvel Team-Up #103 (1980)

Cover Artist: Frank Miller

Daredevil may be Frank Miller’s signature Marvel character, but just as his DD run became one of the defining comics of the early 1980s, Miller also contributed artwork to several other books, including this cover of Marvel Team-Up, drawn at such an extreme low angel that it really accentuates the power of Taskmaster and the tininess of the month’s special guest star, Ant-Man.

Marvel

39. The Amazing Spider-Man #12 (1964)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

This one’s a veritable checklist of great Spider-Man cover tropes combined into a single image:

✅ Spider-Man unmasked
✅ In front of his love interest
✅ And J. Jonah Jameson
✅ Defeated by one of his arch-enemies
✅ On the verge of arrest by the police

These elements would get mixed and matched endlessly over the next six decades, although rarely with the panache and drama of the great Steve Ditko.

Marvel

38. Avenging Spider-Man #14 (2012)

Cover Artist: Gabriele Dell’Otto

Avenging Spider-Man was a modern variant of the old Marvel Team-Up format: Each issue, Spider-Man got partnered with a different guest star. In this issue, he meets the oddball Jack Kirby creations Moon Boy and Devil Dinosaur. Gabriele Dell’Otto’s dynamic cover at demonstrates that this will not be one of Spidey’s most harmonious partnerships.

Marvel

37. Spider-Man/Human Torch #4 (2005)

Cover Artist: Paul Smith

Paul Smith, master of facial expressions. Look at that Johnny Storm! The black (or dark blue) and white costumes really pop against the red heart in the background as well.

Marvel

36. The Amazing Spider-Man: Spirits of the Earth (1990)

Cover Artist: Charles Vess

Fantasy artist Charles Vess left his mark on the Spider-Man mythos with this moody graphic novel (plus an even more famous cover we’ll get to later on this list). Countless webs have graced the covers of Spider-Man’s many comics, but the one on Vess’ Spirits of the Earth might be the most convincingly spidery of all of them.

Marvel

35. The Amazing Spider-Man #1 (2014)

Cover Artist: Marcos Martin

Another Marcos Martin banger. The dramatic Spider-Man pose, the inverted perspective, the massive title treatment, the curvature of the Earth suggesting Spidey’s incredible altitude and velocity during this dive ... they’re all working together in perfect harmony.

Marvel

34. Ultimate Spider-Man #13 (2001)

Cover Artist: Mark Bagley

So many Spider-Man comics tease the shocking revelation of Spider-Man’s secret identity, only to use some clever twist to wriggle out of it (See the Ditko cover for The Amazing Spider-Man #12 just a few entries ago on this list.) Ultimate Spider-Man #13 actually made good on that promise, with its version of Peter Parker revealing his secret identity to Mary Jane. At last, an image of Spider-Man without his mask (with MJ’s shocked expression reflected in his mirrored lenses) finally delivered the goods.

Marvel

33. The Amazing Spider-Man #53 (2024)

Cover Artist: Russell Dauterman 

Artist Russell Dauterman is known for his gorgeous “costume variant” covers, where he draws a famous Marvel character in every different costume they’ve ever worn. Every one of these is great — and his Spider-Man costume variant is no exception.

Marvel

32. The Amazing Spider-Man #55 (1967)

Cover Artist: John Romita

Another mirrored lenses masterpiece, this one from Jazzy John Romita. Doctor Octopus: He might be a madman, he might want to conquer humanity, but you gotta admit: The dude has terrific teeth.

Marvel

31. The Spectacular Spider-Man #148 (1989)

Cover Artist: Sal Buscema

If you read Spider-Man comics at all in the 1980s and ’90s, you know the work of Sal Buscema, one of the definitive Spidey artists of that period. He produced a lot of great Spider-Man covers during that period, so there are a lot of worthy candidates for this list. There’s more of his work to come, but I had to include this one, because it was another cover that sold me as a child looking through a convenience store spinner rack. You don’t need to know who Ned Leeds is (or get the Night of the Living Dead reference) to want to read the story inside.

Marvel

30. The Amazing Spider-Man #237 (1982)

Cover Artist: Ed Hannigan

Stilt Man might be the dumbest Marvel villain ever. (He has really long stilts. That’s it. That’s his whole deal.) But he sure looks like a major star on this Ed Hannigan cover, thanks to the way he’s destroying the book’s title (and even the “Marvel Comics Group” banner) with his blaster.

Marvel

29. Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #119 (1986)

Cover Artist: Rich Buckler

Similar to our last cover, which showed a character bursting through a comic’s logo, this ferocious piece by artist Rich Buckler shows X-Men villain Sabretooth tearing through the entire cover of Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #119. If you didn’t know who this character was because you didn’t read X-Men comics, this single image tells you he is a seriously dangerous foe. Bonus points for distending the image of Spider-Man to give the rips the look of authentic paper.

Marvel

28. Spider-Man: Blue #2 (2002)

Cover Artist: Tim Sale

The late, great Tim Sale and writer Jeph Loeb followed their acclaimed DC books Batman: The Long Halloween and Dark Victory with a quartet of thematically linked miniseries about major Marvel heroes during their early years of crimefighting. Spider-Man: Blue is about how the memory of Gwen Stacy still hangs over Peter Parker’s life, a concept encapsulated perfectly by Sale’s spare cover to Blue’s second issue.

Marvel

27. Daredevil/Spider-Man #2 (2000)

Cover Artist: Alex Ross

While Alex Ross is known for his painterly portraits of iconic Marvel and DC heroes, he’s no slouch when it comes to more dynamic images. This beautifully symmetrical piece from 2000’s Daredevil/Spider-Man miniseries stands out as one of the finest examples of that kind of work.

Marvel

26. The Amazing Spider-Man #3 (1963)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

Doctor Octopus debuts in this book-length super-thriller (!) adorned with a shadowy, ominous, atmospheric Steve Ditko cover befitting “America’s most exciting super-hero” and “the world’s most dreaded super-villain!”

Marvel

25. Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #109 (1985)

Cover Artist: Rich Buckler

The introduction of Spider-Man’s black costume encourage Marvel artists to take the character’s artwork in noirish new dimensions. Here Rich Buckler depicts a powerful (but also slightly threatening) Spider-Man high atop a New York City skyscraper in a tableau of black, white, and red that suggests this issue will contain plenty of darkness and bloodshed.

Marvel

24. The Amazing Spider-Man #1 (1962)

Cover Artist: Jack Kirby

Jack Kirby never served as a regular artist on Spider-Man’s adventures but he illustrated both of his first two covers, including the debut issue of The Amazing Spider-Man, which featured an appearance by the Fantastic Four to maximize interest in the new hero. Kirby’s Spider-Man looks powerful yet suitably inhuman, and the swooping Human Torch blazing from the background all the way to the piece’s front left corner adds a lot of kinetic energy to a static cover.

Marvel

23. The Amazing Spider-Man #43 (2002)

Cover Artist: John Romita Jr.

John Romita Jr. — son of definitive Spider-Man artist John Romita — has contributed about as much to the visual canon of Spider-Man as any person in history, with great runs on the character across 40 years. His consistently striking and dramatic Spidey covers include this rain-soaked piece from the early 2000s.

Marvel

22. Spider-Man #1 (1990)

Cover Artist: Todd McFarlane

Todd McFarlane so captivated Marvel readers with his exaggerated and hyperflexible vision of Spider-Man that he earned his own monthly series, simply titled Spider-Man, that he wrote and illustrated. The first issue sold a whopping 2.5 million copies, making it one of the biggest comics in history — and making this one of the most-seen Spider-Man covers in history to boot.

Marvel

21. The Amazing Spider-Man #121 (1973)

Cover Artist: John Romita

John Romita brings Spider-Man to a major TURNING POINT — the death of a key member of his supporting cast, heralded by this headshot-filled cover that tantalizes readers with the promise that one of the nine faces strewn around Spidey will die before the issue’s conclusion.

Marvel

20. The Spectacular Spider-Man #142 (1988)

Cover Artist: Sal Buscema

Another Sal Buscema classic, this one depicting Spidey dangling from a truly vertiginous height. Spider-Man baddie Tombstone has never looked better either, with his chalk-white skin contrasting with his dapper dark suit. His menacing grin is a lovely detail as well.

Marvel

19. Peter Parker: Spider-Man #35 (2001)

Cover Artist: Humberto Ramos

Comic-book covers do not exist in a commercial vacuum. They’re expected to not only look good but also to convince the potential costumer to plunk down their five bucks to read the story inside. As such, they tend to rely on exaggerated images of extreme excitement. They rarely attempt what artist Humberto Ramos did so successfully here: To emphasize that Spider-Man’s greatest power is his selfless dedication to helping others. Sometimes the most heroic thing a person can do is listen to someone in their time of need — and that is what Ramos conveys on his cover for Peter Parker: Spider-Man #35.

Marvel

18. The Amazing Spider-Man #238 (1982)

Cover Artist: John Romita Jr.

The Hobgoblin debuted in this issue, adorned with a sinister piece by John Romita Jr. (Also: How do I get me some of those FREE Lakeside Skin Tattooz??)

Marvel

17. The Superior Spider-Man #9 (2013)

Cover Artist: Marcos Martin

Superior Spider-Man was an epic storyline about Doctor Octopus’ ultimate plan for revenge against his arch-enemy. Eventually, Ock manages to implant his consciousness into Peter Parker’s brain, taking control of his body and his amazing spider powers. It initially appears that Peter’s mind and soul have been permanently killed — but this is comics, so of course he eventually reemerges and attempts to reassert control over his body. The battle of wills that follows plays out across Peter and Ock’s shared mindscape, and there couldn’t possibly be a better cover to summarize all of that than Marcos Martin’s for Superior Spider-Man #9.

Marvel

16. The Amazing Spider-Man #68 (1968)

Cover Artist: John Romita

When I was in my early teens, my father gave me what remained of his own childhood comic-book collection. He had a bunch of Justice League of America issues of the 1960s, and a few early Marvel books. I read them all, and my favorite of the bunch of The Amazing Spider-Man #68, which sported this absolutely gorgeous John Romita cover. Clearly, I’m not the only one who thinks it is magnificent; Todd McFarlane’s toy company recreated it in statue form a few years ago.

Marvel

15. The Amazing Spider-Man #196 (1979)

Cover Artist: Keith Pollard

Aunt May has appeared to die several times through the decades, only to return, alive and well, every single time. That doesn’t diminish the power of covers like this one on The Amazing Spider-Man #196, depicting a devastated Peter Parker mourning over May’s grave, while Spider-Man’s silhouette looms in the background. All the little touches here — the shadow cast by Peter over the headstone, the gnarled, leafless tree twisting its way toward the sky — add to the ambiance of death and darkness as well.

Marvel

14. Ultimate Six #5 (2003)

Cover Artist: John Cassaday

Sandman is one of Spider-Man’s signature villains, with dozens of appearances across the character’s decades of comics. And to my mind, this is his signature cover. Instead of a dude in a green and black T-shirt and a weird haircut, you have this sentient desert coming to claim our hero with countless, grainy hands. It’s a literally and metaphorically gritty image by the late John Cassady, one of his generation’s definitive comic artists.

Marvel

13. Amazing Spider-Man #316 (1989)

Cover Artist: Todd McFarlane

How good is this Todd McFarlane cover of Venom pouncing on a prone Spider-Man? So good you still see it reprinter on merchandise and T-shirts to this day.

Marvel

12. Amazing Spider-Man #293 (1987)

Cover Artist: Mike Zeck

Just about every issue of the famous “Kraven’s Last Hunt” storyline, in which the title character manages to defeat and temporarily replace Spider-Man, featured a cover worthy of inclusion on this list. But if I can only pick one of them, I’ll go with this incredible Mike Zeck piece that boasts incredible atmosphere (the rain and lightning), a ferocious Kraven howling to the dark night sky, and the mystery of why he holds Spider-Man’s empty costume — along with that oversized gravestone that bears the words “Here Lies Spider-Man, Slain by The Hunter.”

Marvel

11. Untold Tales of Spider-Man #19 (1997)

Cover Artist: Pat Olliffe

A superior variation on that Web of Spider-Man cover with the clueless loved one of Peter Parker inside a house while unbeknownst to them Spider-Man lurks just outside the window. This version by Pat Olliffe heightens every aspect of the conceit, with Spider-Man actively fighting Doctor Octopus on the roof of Aunt May’s home while she frets about him because he’s so “frail.”

Marvel

10. The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #15 (1981)

Cover Artist: Frank Miller

This Frank Miller cover for The Amazing Spider-Man Annual #15 puts you into the perspective of Doctor Octopus as he examines the cover of the latest issue of the Daily Bugle, which features a bold image of Spider-Man locked in battle with the Punisher. It sets up an intriguing three-way power struggle between the characters. Plenty of artists could draw something similar, but only an artist as witty and thoughtful as Miller would include a touch like the steaming cup of coffee in one of Ock’s metal tentacles, as if this is just an ordinary Saturday morning around the breakfast table for ol’ Ock.

Marvel

9. Web of Spider-Man #1 (1984)

Cover Artist: Charles Vess

In 1985, Marvel replaced their third monthly Spider-Man title, Marvel Team-Up, with a new book called Web of Spider-Man. While Web of Spider-Man rarely equaled its higher-profile predecessors, its first issue boasted one of the great Spider-Man covers of all time, this evocative cityscape featuring a black-suited Peter Parker perched on a foggy rooftop.

Marvel

8. The Amazing Spider-Man #129 (1973)

Cover Artist: Gil Kane

Talk about a new character making a big impact. The Punisher’s splashy debut came in 1973’s The Amazing Spider-Man #129, where he put the Friendly Neighborhood Wall-Crawler directly in his crosshairs on this explosive Gil Kane cover.

Marvel

7. The Amazing Spider-Man #52 (2003)

Cover Artist: J. Scott Campbell﻿

The wedge that Spider-Man drives between Peter Parker and the people he loves looms over most of the best Spidey stories. J. Scott Campbell turns that concept into the haunting centerpiece of this cover from the early 2000s. While Mary Jane waits for her husband in a warm apartment, Spider-Man climbs on the exterior of the building during a chilly snowstorm. Without even knowing it, Peter and MJ’s hands are each touching the exact same point on the wall — but his double life has literally come between their chance for domestic bliss.

Marvel

6. The Amazing Spider-Man #39 (1966)

Cover Artist: John Romita

Here’s one of the great “OH S—!” moments in Marvel Comics history; when Green Goblin discovered Peter Parker’s secret identity. John Romita’s cover for the landmark Amazing Spider-Man #39 amps up the element of danger by depicting Peter captured by the Goblin, his civilian clothes shredded as he’s dangled preciously on a Goblin Glider ride over Manhattan.

Marvel

5. The Amazing Spider-Man #258 (1984)

Cover Artist: Ron Frenz

At the height of the drama surrounding Spider-Man’s new alien costume, Ron Frenz — maybe the most underrated Spider-Man artist in the character’s history — delivered a cover for the ages, a nightmare scenario depicting Peter at war with both his new and old costumes as all three fall into a swirling abyss. Something about the way the costumes are flat and empty makes the fact that they are overpowering him that much more disturbing.

Marvel

4. Peter Parker, The Spectacular Spider-Man #101 (1985)

Cover Artist: John Byrne

Although most fans were lukewarm on John Byrne’s run as the primary Spider-Man writer and artist in the late 1990s, Byrne will always have this piece on his resume, one of the coolest and most eye-catching covers in the character’s history. The high-contrast piece features Spider-Man in his black costume in mid-somersault, swooping through an entirely black-and-white New York cityscape. It’s absolutely gorgeous; I would love to see an entire comic rendered in this style.

Marvel

3. The Amazing Spider-Man #33 (1965)

Cover Artist: Steve Ditko

To this day, The Amazing Spider-Man #33 contains maybe the most famous sequence in any issue of any Spider-Man comic. After a battle with Doctor Octopus, Spider-Man gets buried beneath an unimaginably heavy pile of rubble. No one alive could lift it, not even a Spider-Man — but if he quits then Aunt May dies, because Peter is the only one with a serum that can save her. Over several pages, Peter gives himself a pep talk in the form of an epic soliloquy, with Steve Ditko mining every second for maximum suspense. His cover for the issue, with a tiny Spidey surrounded by steel and rising waters, with the caption “The FINAL CHAPTER!” is the icing on the cake of this Marvel masterpiece.

Marvel

2. The Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962)

Cover Artist: Jack Kirby

Marvel’s early ’60s anthology series Amazing Fantasy was already slated for cancelation by its 15th issue, when writer Stan Lee snuck in a concept he’d been tinkering with for a while: A superhero strip where a teenage was the star rather than the sidekick. (Marvel chief Martin Goodman supposedly hated the concept, but allowed Lee to try it, because Amazing Fantasy was already on the chopping block anyway.) After Stan Lee rejected Steve Ditko’s original cover for the issue, he recruited Jack Kirby to pencil a replacement. I’m going to say he nailed the assignment. His eye-catching cover helped propel Amazing Fantasy #15 to surprisingly solid sales and ecstatic reader feedback, prompting the character’s return in his own Amazing Spider-Man series.

Marvel

1. The Amazing Spider-Man #50 (1967)

Cover Artist: John Romita

Every single Spider-Man story is about the battle between Peter Parker and his costumed alter ego. The tension in the book for over 60 years comes from the fact that if Spider-Man succeeds, it invariably costs Peter Parker something dear — Spidey defeats the Green Goblin, but Gwen Stacy dies in the battle — or vice versa — Peter goes out on a date with Mary Jane, but while he does so the Vulture steals an experimental de-aging technology. It’s a heightened version of an utterly mundane dilemma: Each individual’s eternal struggle to decide how much of their lives to devote to their personal desires and their professional responsibilities. Do I play video games tonight or do I finish my homework? Do I visit my ailing aunt or hang out with my college buddies? Do I mow the lawn or drink a beer?

That conflict has formed the basis for a lot of Spider-Man covers over the years as well, but no one did it better than John Romita on The Amazing Spider-Man #50. His piece is a heightened variation of the image that concluded many of Spider-Man’s earliest stories: A detected Peter Parker walking off alone into the night after another personal disaster. This time, Peter walks toward the reader, his head slumped down in a posture of utter defeat, while a massive Spider-Man turns his back on him.

Of course Spider-Man will never be “no more!” as long as the books and movies and toys keep selling. But for 60 years, this image has stood as one of the signature works in the Spider-Man canon. And because that same eternal inner struggle continues within all of us, John Romita’s often-imitated Spider-Man cover will never get old.
